summary.title: Concurrent Servers: Part 3 - Event-driven
summary.one_liner: You learn how nonblocking I/O, polling and the select() system call enable a single-threaded, event-driven network server that handles many clients concurrently.
keywords: how to handle many clients in c
takeaways: Nonblocking recv returns immediately with EAGAIN/EWOULDBLOCK when no data is ready, but polling this way wastes CPU and scales poorly.
select() lets one thread watch many file descriptors for readiness, and the caller must keep master fd_sets because select overwrites them.
An event-driven server is built from callbacks invoked by a main loop; callbacks must never block and must keep partial-data state between calls.
select is synchronous as an API (it blocks), yet the server design it enables is asynchronous/callback-based.
select has limits: FD_SETSIZE is usually 1024 on modern systems and it performs poorly with very many descriptors.
summary.summary: The post is part 3 of a series on concurrent network servers. It starts by contrasting blocking and nonblocking recv with a pair of small C listener programs, showing that polling a nonblocking socket works but wastes CPU and scales badly. It then introduces select() for I/O multiplexing, walking through the fd_set contract and a complete single-threaded select-based server with read and send callbacks and a per-peer state machine. The post closes by clarifying the terminology (synchronous vs asynchronous, callback-based, event-driven) and listing select's limitations, such as the fixed FD_SETSIZE and poor performance at large descriptor counts.
